gloss: A physical activity played by rules for competition or fun.
examples: Soccer is the only *sport* he really follows.
The school offers a dozen different *sports* in the fall.
Swimming is a good *sport* for people with bad knees.
contrast: Americans say *sports* where the British say *sport*: he plays sports vs. he plays sport.

gloss: A contest played by set rules, or one single contest in a series.
examples: We won the *game* by three points.
There are two *games* left in the season.
Chess is a *game* of patience.

gloss: A single contest between two players or two teams.
examples: The tennis *match* went on for four hours.
Both *matches* got rained out.
He lost the *match* in straight sets.

gloss: The game played on a large field by two sides of eleven who move the ball mostly with their feet.
examples: My daughter plays *soccer* on Saturdays.
*Soccer* is finally getting decent TV ratings here.
He coached youth *soccer* for ten years.
contrast: *Soccer* is the American name for the game the rest of the world calls football.

ru: американский футбол; мяч для этой игры
countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The American game played with an oval ball and helmets, or the ball used in it.
examples: He played *football* in high school.
Somebody left two *footballs* out in the rain.
*Football* season starts in September.
contrast: In the US *football* means American football; the game played with the feet is *soccer*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The indoor game in which two teams of five throw a ball through a raised hoop, or the ball itself.
examples: She has a full ride for *basketball*.
The gym had a bin of worn-out *basketballs*.
We watched college *basketball* all weekend.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The American game played with a bat and a small hard ball, or that ball.
examples: *Baseball* is still my dad's favorite sport.
He keeps a shelf of signed *baseballs*.
We have *baseball* tickets for Friday.

gloss: A fast game played on ice in which players hit a rubber disk into the other team's goal.
examples: He's played *hockey* since he was five.
*Hockey* is huge in Minnesota.
They watch *hockey* every Saturday night.

gloss: A game in which two or four players hit a ball over a net with rackets.
examples: Do you want to play *tennis* on Sunday?
She took up *tennis* after she retired.
*Tennis* is easier on your knees than running.

gloss: A game in which players hit a small ball into a series of holes with clubs.
examples: My boss talks about *golf* nonstop.
He plays *golf* every Saturday morning.
*Golf* eats up an entire afternoon.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A game in which two teams hit a ball back and forth over a high net, or the ball used.
examples: We played beach *volleyball* until it got dark.
The equipment closet is full of flat *volleyballs*.
She got a scholarship for *volleyball*.

gloss: The sport of fighting with padded gloves inside a roped ring.
examples: He took up *boxing* to get in shape.
*Boxing* isn't as popular as it used to be.
There's a *boxing* gym two blocks from here.

gloss: The sport of gripping an opponent and trying to pin him to the mat.
examples: *Wrestling* practice starts at six in the morning.
She got into *wrestling* in middle school.
College *wrestling* has strict weight classes.

gloss: The activity or sport of moving through water with your arms and legs.
examples: *Swimming* is the best workout for your back.
She quit *swimming* after high school.
There's no *swimming* allowed after dark.

gloss: The activity or sport of moving fast on foot for exercise or in a race.
examples: *Running* wrecked my knees.
He got into *running* after he turned forty.
*Running* on a treadmill bores me to death.

gloss: The sport or activity of riding a bicycle.
examples: *Cycling* is big in this part of the state.
She switched from running to *cycling*.
Indoor *cycling* classes fill up fast.

gloss: The sport of moving over snow on long narrow boards attached to your boots.
examples: We go *skiing* every February.
*Skiing* out west is a whole different thing.
He gave up *skiing* after he broke his leg.
contrast: Keep both i's: ski + -ing spells *skiing*, and it is two syllables, SKEE-ing.

gloss: The activity of moving on ice or pavement wearing skates.
examples: The pond is finally hard enough for *skating*.
Figure *skating* takes years of lessons.
There's public *skating* every Friday night.

gloss: The sport of riding ocean waves standing on a board.
examples: He drove down the coast for the *surfing*.
*Surfing* looks easy until you try it.
The *surfing* is best early in the morning.

gloss: The sport of going up rock or walls using your hands and feet.
examples: Indoor *climbing* got her over her fear of heights.
He's into rock *climbing* now.
*Climbing* is harder on your fingers than you'd think.
contrast: The *b* is silent: KLY-ming, not KLIMB-ing.

gloss: The game of rolling a heavy ball down a lane to knock over pins.
examples: *Bowling* is the only sport my whole family will do.
There's a *bowling* alley by the mall.
We went *bowling* for his birthday.

gloss: The sport of jumping headfirst into water, or of swimming underwater with tanks.
examples: She won a medal in *diving*.
Scuba *diving* is expensive to get into.
The pool is too shallow for *diving*.

gloss: A system of stretches, poses, and breathing done for fitness and calm.
examples: *Yoga* fixed my lower back.
She teaches *yoga* on Tuesday nights.
I do twenty minutes of *yoga* before work.

gloss: A Japanese martial art of fighting with sharp blows of the hands and feet.
examples: Both kids take *karate* after school.
He has a black belt in *karate*.
*Karate* taught her more discipline than anything else.
contrast: The final *e* is pronounced: kuh-RAH-tee, not kuh-RAHT.

gloss: A board game for two players using sixteen pieces each on a checkered board.
examples: My grandfather taught me *chess*.
He plays *chess* online every night.
*Chess* is having a real moment right now.

gloss: A rough team game played with an oval ball that players carry, kick, and pass backward.
examples: He played *rugby* in college.
*Rugby* never really caught on here.
There's a *rugby* club that practices in the park.

gloss: A running race of just over twenty-six miles.
examples: She finished her first *marathon* in four hours.
He's run six *marathons* since he turned fifty.
Training for a *marathon* takes about four months.

gloss: Someone who takes part in a game or sport.
examples: He's the best *player* on the team.
Two *players* got hurt in the first half.
She's a solid *player*, just not a star.

gloss: The official who enforces the rules during a game.
examples: The *referee* called a foul on the play.
Both *referees* missed it.
Nobody wants to be a *referee* in youth soccer.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable: ref-uh-REE.

gloss: The official who calls plays in baseball, tennis, and some other sports.
examples: The *umpire* threw him out of the game.
Both *umpires* agreed the ball was foul.
He argued with the *umpire* for ten minutes.

gloss: The person or team that finishes first in a competition.
examples: She's the defending *champion*.
The *champions* got a parade downtown.
He was a state wrestling *champion* in high school.

gloss: The person or team you are playing against.
examples: His *opponent* was a foot taller.
They studied film on their next three *opponents*.
Never underestimate an *opponent* you don't know.

gloss: A team or person you compete against again and again.
examples: We play our biggest *rival* on Friday.
The two *rivals* have met in the final four times.
He beat his old *rival* in three sets.

gloss: Someone who follows and supports a team, player, or sport.
examples: I've been a *fan* since I was a kid.
Thousands of *fans* showed up in the rain.
He's a huge hockey *fan*.

gloss: Someone who watches an event without taking part.
examples: *Spectators* had to stay behind the fence.
One *spectator* ran onto the field.
It's a great *spectator* sport.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, SPEK-tay-tur; the British say spek-TAY-tuh.

gloss: The player whose job is to keep the ball or puck out of the goal.
examples: Their *goalie* stopped forty shots.
Both *goalies* played the whole game.
He's been a *goalie* since he was eight.

gloss: The baseball player who throws the ball to the batter.
examples: Their starting *pitcher* left in the fifth inning.
They went through four *pitchers* in one game.
He was a *pitcher* in high school.
contrast: Don't confuse it with *picture* (PIK-chur) — *pitcher* has no k sound.

gloss: The football player who directs the attack and throws most of the passes.
examples: Their *quarterback* threw three touchdowns.
Two *quarterbacks* went down with injuries.
He's the best *quarterback* they've had in years.

gloss: Someone who fights in the sport of boxing.
examples: The *boxer* went down in the third round.
Both *boxers* made weight.
He trains amateur *boxers* on weekends.

gloss: Someone who swims, especially in competition.
examples: She's the fastest *swimmer* on the team.
The *swimmers* were in the pool by five.
He's a strong *swimmer* but a terrible runner.

gloss: Someone who guides a person's training or treats athletes' injuries.
examples: She hired a personal *trainer* in January.
The *trainer* taped his ankle at halftime.
Both *trainers* work with the football team.
contrast: In Britain *trainers* also means sneakers; in the US it only means a person.

gloss: A player in his or her first season on a professional team.
examples: The *rookie* scored twenty points in his first start.
Three *rookies* made the roster.
For a *rookie*, she's incredibly calm.

gloss: Someone who plays on the same team as you.
examples: His *teammates* carried him off the field.
She's a good *teammate* even when she isn't playing.
Two former *teammates* now coach against each other.

gloss: The team or player everyone expects to lose.
examples: Nobody minds rooting for the *underdog*.
They went in as ten-point *underdogs* and won.
She's the *underdog* in every match she plays.

gloss: Someone who runs, especially as a sport.
examples: He's a long-distance *runner*.
Thousands of *runners* lined up at the start.
She's the fastest *runner* in her grade.
